logline: Two rival geniuses - one serving a crumbling galactic empire, the other defending a corrupt democracy - wage war across the stars while questioning whether the system they fight for deserves to survive.

renewal.note: The classic 1988-1997 OVA series (110 episodes across four seasons plus two Gaiden OVA series) concluded its run in 1997. A remake series, Die Neue These, launched in 2018 and continues separately.

bollymeter.basis: ANN weighted mean of 8.838 (Excellent) from 792 raters, ranked #13 of all anime ever catalogued. Median rating is Masterpiece - the series is regarded by a significant portion of its audience as the finest long-form anime ever made.

seasons.review_body: The first season of the OVA, released directly to home video from December 1988, introduced what many critics now consider anime's greatest science-fiction epic. Kitty Films and Artland adapted Yoshiki Tanaka's novel series into a work of unusual political and philosophical ambition, building two fully realised ideological blocs - the autocratic Galactic Empire and the nominally democratic Free Planets Alliance - and mapping their centuries-long conflict through two rival commanders. ANN's weighted mean of 8.838 (ranked #13 all-time from 792 ratings) and a median of Masterpiece reflect a consensus that the first season establishes the template: long strategic sequences, literate dialogue, and an unflinching willingness to kill consequential characters without melodrama. IMDb's 9.0 from a wider audience pool confirms the reverence is not cult-narrow. The show is unhurried by design; episodes read as chapters in a novel rather than event television, and the first season's patience is exactly what earns the later episodes their weight.

episode_reviews.title: In the Eternal Night (Prologue)
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The opening episode establishes both protagonists and the scale of the war between Empire and Alliance in a single fleet engagement. The show refuses to tell you who to root for - both sides are argued with equal intelligence.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The battle map sequence showing the true scale of interstellar war - this is not a metaphor, it is the actual argument the series will make for 110 episodes.

bollymeter.basis: The political machinery tightens in Season 2 as Reinhard consolidates power inside the Empire and Yang faces bureaucratic obstruction from his own government - critics consider this the series' ideological core.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 deepens the structural critique that Season 1 planted. Reinhard von Lohengramm's campaign to centralise imperial power and Yang Wen-li's growing disillusionment with the Alliance's democratic machinery run in parallel, and the series resists the temptation to favour either. The 28 episodes push into territory most anime avoids entirely - the epistemology of political loyalty, the institutional mechanisms that corrupt ideals, and the human cost of ideological purity. The lack of a conventional hero makes the season harder to parse for newcomers but more rewarding for viewers who have accepted the show's terms. Multiple sequences with no action at all - only dialogue between strategists - rank among the most gripping the medium has produced. ANN's weighted mean of 8.838 and a Masterpiece median rating reflect an audience that places this arc at the series' philosophical core.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 2 pivots from introducing the conflict to interrogating the systems that sustain it - more talk, more philosophy, higher stakes, and considerably more ruthless about consequences.

bollymeter.basis: Season 3 is where the 100-episode investment pays the highest dividend - critics describe the climactic events as among the most satisfying resolutions in all of anime.

seasons.review_body: At 32 episodes, Season 3 is the longest and most consequential leg of the OVA run. The political upheavals seeded across the previous two seasons resolve here in ways the series earns through accumulated detail rather than plot convenience. The series is described in contemporaneous critical accounts as having one of the most satisfying endings in anime - and Season 3 is where that trajectory locks in. The Alliance storyline reaches its structural crisis; the Empire storyline accelerates toward Reinhard's singular ambition. What separates the show from lesser space operas is that neither outcome feels determined by editorial preference - the logic of each political system produces its own collapse. Season 3 is not the place to start but it is the reason to complete the journey.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 3 is the fulcrum: the longest run, the largest events, and the moments that explain why critics call this one of the most satisfying anime endings ever written.

bollymeter.basis: The final season closes the epic without softening its conclusions. Critics note that the series never loses its refusal to romanticise power even in its final frames.

seasons.review_body: The fourth and final season of the original OVA ran 24 episodes and concluded in March 1997. It closes the twin arcs without concession to sentimentality - the series has been teaching its audience for 110 episodes that history does not reward the virtuous or punish the wicked by any consistent moral logic, and the finale does not contradict that thesis. The animation quality of the concluding season was superior to the late-1980s opening episodes, reflecting nearly a decade of production. ANN users who rated the OVA as a whole - giving it a Masterpiece median - typically describe the ending as proof that the length was justified. Season 4 works only as the culmination of what preceded it; watched in isolation it would be incomprehensible. As a conclusion, it is one of the few long-form anime finales that matches the ambition of its premise.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 4 resolves the 110-episode arc with the same philosophical refusal to sentimentalise that defined the series from its first episode.
